title: Amended Notarisation Law from 1 January 2027: What Is New
desc: Law No. 04/2026/QH16 amending the Notarisation Law, effective 1 January 2027: e-dossiers, data retrieval, property notarisation, powers of attorney.
summary: Summary of the new points in Law No. 04/2026/QH16 amending the Notarisation Law (effective 1 January 2027) that buyers, sellers, donors and grantors of powers of attorney over property should know.
body: On 23 April 2026, the National Assembly passed Law No. 04/2026/QH16 amending and supplementing a number of articles of the Notarisation Law. The Law is not yet in force and will apply from 1 January 2027 (Article 2). Until the end of 2026 the 2024 Notarisation Law continues to apply. Below are the changes that bear directly on property transactions.

From 1 January 2027, the amending Law defines notarisation as a public service performed by a notary to certify the authenticity and legality of a transaction in writing that must be notarised or that an individual or organisation voluntarily requests. Notaries are appointed by the Chairperson of the provincial People's Committee (Clause 1, Article 1).

Transactions that must be notarised are important transactions that require strict participation conditions and a high degree of legal safety and that are prescribed by law as requiring notarisation. The Ministry of Justice reviews and publishes the list of transactions that must be notarised or certified on the Ministry's web portal (Clause 2, Article 1). The current 2024 Law also allows “the law to assign the Government to prescribe” (Article 3 of the 2024 Notarisation Law). Within 1 year from 1 January 2027, the Government reviews the regulations on transactions that must be notarised (Clause 6, Article 3).
3. Dossier: electronic copies accepted, less paperwork

The dossier consists of the draft transaction, identity papers, the certificate (or a substitute document) and other papers as prescribed; these may be paper copies, electronic copies or electronic originals; they may be submitted online, in person or by post.
Where information is already in a published database, the applicant need not submit that document; if the applicant asks the notary to retrieve it, a data retrieval fee is payable.
A notary may request additional documents only when the information cannot be retrieved within the notarisation time limit or is incomplete or inaccurate.
4. Property notarisation stays provincial, with a nationwide roadmap to come

A notary may still notarise only transactions involving real estate within the province or centrally run city where the notarial practice organisation is headquartered, except for wills, refusals of inheritance and powers of attorney concerning rights over real estate. The Government will prescribe a roadmap for nationwide notarisation once the notarisation database is operating (Clause 13, Article 1, amending Article 44).
5. Powers of attorney when the two parties are in two places

If the principal and the attorney cannot come to the same place, each party has the document notarised at the organisation of its choice. If both parties jointly request notarisation of an amendment, supplement or agreement to terminate the power of attorney contract at one of the two organisations that notarised it earlier, that organisation must notify the other and send it a copy within 5 working days (Clause 15, Article 1, amending Article 57). In addition, the applicant may ask to sign and fingerprint at the same time (Clause 14, Article 1).

The notarisation database contains information on notaries, notarised transactions, the transaction status of assets, preventive measures and risk warnings, and notarised documents; it is built uniformly by the Ministry of Justice from the central to the local level (Clause 16, Article 1). The provincial People's Committee may transfer the authority to certify transactions from the commune-level People's Committee Chairperson to notarial practice organisations in communes that already have a notarial organisation meeting demand (Clause 7, Article 1).
For the current procedure for notarising a sale contract, see Notarising a house and land sale contract in 2026.

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. Law No. 04/2026/QH16 is not yet in force (from 1 January 2027). The 2024 Notarisation Law has been amended by Law No. 106/2025/QH15 (not yet in our library), so the comparison is based on the 2024 Law text in our library. New implementing decrees may add detail.
